#3503. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

#3502. 7 Upcoming Fantasy Shows, Ranked by Hype

2026 has been a pretty solid year for fantasy television. So far, the year has seen new seasons of shows like House of the Dragon and Interview with the Vampire, as well as brand-new series like Avatar: Seven Havens and Witch Hat Atelier. However, as fun as those shows are, there are several exciting fantasy shows in the pipeline right now that could potentially blow those hits out of the water.

With release dates across the rest of 2026, 2027, and beyond, several upcoming shows have garnered sky-high hype among fantasy fans, drumming up lots of conversations ahead of their premieres. Not all of the conversations are positive, of course, and there’s at least one upcoming project that’s been talked about for all the wrong reasons, but on the whole, the future of fantasy television does look pretty bright. Without further ado, here are some of the most fascinating upcoming fantasy shows ranked by hype.

Based on J. K. Rowling’s bestselling fantasy books, Harry Potter is an upcoming fantasy series that’s the second adaptation of the novels after the film series. Starring Dominic McLaughlin as Harry, Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley, and Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger, the show’s first season adapts the first book, Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, and details Harry’s discovery of the wizarding world and his first year at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. The ensemble cast also includes John Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer as Minerva McGonagall, Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape, and Nick Frost as Rubeus Hagrid.

HBO has big plans for Harry Potter, with early reports estimating that the new show could span a decade of production. The series has already been renewed for a second season as well. However, the whole project has been largely met with the opposite of hype. Comparisons to the movies (the last of which came out in 2011), negative public opinion of J.K. Rowling, and the idea that the whole project is a naked cash grab have all led to a generally dismal reception from the core fanbase ahead of the show’s release.

Created by Richard Garfield, Magic: The Gathering is one of the most successful game franchises of all time. A trading card game that’s expanded to various other media, the franchise is set across multiple realities and centered on Planeswalkers, dueling wizards with the ability to cross between worlds. While the game has been adapted as comics and novels before, it’s yet to get a movie or TV adaptation.

The Magic: The Gathering series adaptation has been in development since 2019 and has undergone many behind-the-scenes changes, but it finally looks like the show might actually make it to screens. The new show will be a Netflix animated series with Terry Matalas (12 Monkeys) serving as showrunner. The series was previewed at the 2025 Annecy International Animation Film Festival, but it doesn’t yet have a release date. Nonetheless, fans of the franchise are certainly excited for the show’s release and for the upcoming movie adaptation directed by Matt Johnson (Tony).

One of the bestselling romantasy books of the 2020s, Rebecca Yarros’s Fourth Wing is the first book of the Empyrean new adult fantasy romance series. A series adaptation of the books has been in the works at Prime Video since 2023, with Yarros serving as an executive producer on the project alongside Michael B. Jordan, Lisa Joy, Jonathan Nolan, Liz Pelletier, Athena Wickham, and showrunner Meredith Averill. The show, like the book, follows the story of Violet Sorrengail, who joins the Basgiath War College and trains to become a dragon rider, encountering deadly quests, gruelling competition, and unexpected romance. Esther McGregor will star as Violet, with Emilio Sakraya as her rival/love interest, Xaden Riorson.

Fourth Wing is one of the biggest BookTok hits of the romantasy genre, so its series adaptation has a lot of people very excited, and with good reason. Featuring fast-paced action, high-tension romance, and, of course, dragons, Fourth Wing has all the ingredients to become a fantasy TV landmark to rival Game of Thrones. Whether it will actually achieve that potential remains to be seen.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Mike Flanagan’s The Dark Tower is an upcoming multi-season series adaptation of the fantasy book series by Stephen King. Published between 1982 and 2012, the books revolve around Roland Deschain, a gunslinger on an unending quest across a surreal landscape in search of the titular tower, which sits at the center of a vast multiverse. The books were previously adapted as a 2017 film, which was widely panned by critics, but the series is a complete reboot of the story, and it’s been reported that it will star Sam Strike and Jasper Pääkkönen.

Spanning eight connected novels, one novella, a children’s book, and connections to almost all of King’s celebrated novels, The Dark Tower is the holy grail of Stephen King adaptations. It’s easy to see why the upcoming series has so many people excited, even though it doesn’t have a release date or any concrete details as yet. What little we know about The Dark Tower so far suggests an in-depth adaptation that could prove to be Flanagan’s most ambitious project yet and one of the most fascinating fantasy shows ever made. Or, like the movie, it could just be an expensive failure; only time will tell.

It’s no exaggeration to say that Brandon Sanderson is one of the biggest names in fantasy literature today, and The Stormlight Archive novel series, part of Sanderson’s Cosmere universe, is one of the author’s most popular hits. Currently comprising five novels and two novellas (with plans for a total of 10 novels), it’s an expansive saga set on the battered world of Roshar, which is threatened by magical storms, political tensions, and a looming cataclysm. The books have already inspired a VR experience and a tabletop game, and will soon become an Apple TV series.

As part of Sanderson’s deal with the streaming platform, the author will be personally leading adaptations of his Mistborn novels and The Stormlight Archive, the first as a movie and the second as a TV show, the first season of which will consist of 10 episodes. It’s still early days — the project doesn’t even have a showrunner yet — but it’s easily one of the most hotly anticipated fantasy shows currently in development. With complex character dynamics, intricate worldbuilding, and a fascinating magic system, The Stormlight Archive series has all the potential to become one of the biggest fantasy shows of all time, though, of course, right now, that’s all just speculation.

Developed by Sony Pictures Television, Amazon MGM Studios, and PlayStation Productions, Prime Video’s God of War is the first series adaptation of the video game franchise. Based on the franchise’s Norse mythology era, the show follows Kratos and his son Atreus on a journey to the highest peak of the nine realms, where they hope to spread the ashes of their wife and mother, Faye. Ronald D. Moore serves as the showrunner, and the series stars Dave Bautista and Callum Vinson as Kratos and Atreus, respectively.

God of War fans have been waiting for a live-action adaptation for a long time, and the series is quite highly anticipated as a result. The production has had some significant delays, with original Kratos actor Ryan Hurst suffering an injury during filming, which has prompted a recasting and reshoots. We don’t know when the show will finally arrive, but Prime Video has given it a two-season order, and production is currently expected to end sometime in October 2027.

The second anime adaptation of Eiichiro Oda’s One Piece, The One Piece is a new original net animation show produced by Studio Wit and set to release on Netflix in February 2027. The series is a fresh reboot of the franchise adapted directly from the manga (not the iconic 1999 anime), and it will follow the adventures of Monkey D. Luffy (Mayumi Tanaka), an aspiring pirate who sets out in search of the titular treasure alongside his motley crew, the Straw Hats. Directed by Masashi Koizuka and written by Taku Kishimoto, with character designs by Kyoji Asano and Takatoshi Honda, the show’s seven-episode first season will adapt the first 50 chapters of the manga.

One Piece is one of those anime/manga franchises that’s so big it’s recognizable even to people who’ve never seen an anime before, so it’s pretty understandable why Wit’s The One Piece is so highly anticipated. The new adaptation is expected to fix the classic anime’s pacing issues and elevate the animation style, giving the manga the fully modernized adaptation it deserves and bringing a new generation of viewers to the franchise.

#3501. Every Main Dragon Ball Villain, Ranked From Weakest To Strongest

A memorable villain needs more than overwhelming strength to leave a lasting impression. Compelling motivations, a meaningful role in the story, and a personality that commands attention all help turn an antagonist into an unforgettable character. However, in Dragon Ball, raw power has always been a particularly important part of the equation. From ruthless conquerors to seemingly unstoppable beings capable of threatening entire universes, the franchise has built its reputation on introducing enemies who push Goku and the Z Fighters beyond their limits.

As the series has expanded, so too has its understanding of just how powerful a character can become. Each new era has brought increasingly dangerous opponents, with Dragon Ball Super raising the stakes through gods, multiversal tournaments, and warriors whose abilities challenge even the strongest fighters in Universe 7. Not every character on this list is an outright villain, but each has stood against Goku and his allies or represented an extraordinary threat. Ranked by their demonstrated abilities and overall destructive potential, these are the most powerful antagonists and rivals in Dragon Ball history.

Emperor Pilaf, or as he calls himself, the Great King Pilaf, is the first major villain in Dragon Ball. Pilaf leads a small group consisting of Shu, a ninja dog, and Mai, a female weapons expert and the most competent of the group, and their goal is to gather the Dragon Balls to conquer the world and amass wealth.

Pilaf's plans to make a wish on the Dragon Balls are always frustrated. Pilaf even released King Piccolo to make him his ally, but it didn't go in his favor. Although Pilaf and his gang are weak, serving as comic relief, their greatest ability is their high resistance and perseverance, since they always manage to survive and continue causing trouble.

The Red Ribbon Army in Dragon Ball was formed by powerful members like General Blue, who even defeated Krillin before being stopped by Goku. The Red Ribbon Army was led by Commander Red, who, after revealing the real nature of the organization, was killed by Staff Officer Black. He was later known as Commander Black.

Commander Black wasn't particularly powerful or brave, but he was able to take on Goku by piloting a special battle jacket. This battle jacket could even phase through buildings, fire vaporizing lasers, fly, and drop bombs. However, Goku was able to easily defeat him with a Kamehameha. In Dragon Ball: The Path to Power, Commander Black even killed Android 8.

King Piccolo was one of the toughest enemies Goku fought in the original Dragon Ball anime. King Piccolo was especially evil with a lust for power and incredible strength after he managed to rejuvenate himself. King Piccolo could also control the minds of others, causing many deaths, including those of Krillin, Chiaotzu, and Master Roshi.

Goku's battle against King Piccolo was one of the most brutal in Dragon Ball, where the little hero defeated him with his last bit of strength. King Piccolo lost after being overconfident in his victory. However, King Piccolo's reign of terror marked a before and after in Dragon Ball, focusing more on action and battles and introducing increasingly stronger enemies.

An android created by Dr. Gero by synthesizing cells from various characters. Initially, Cell didn't pose much of a threat. However, he was able to evolve into other forms and gain great powers each time. Cell reached his perfect form after absorbing Android 17 and Android 18, becoming a seemingly invincible villain, unmatched even by Vegeta and Future Trunks.

As Perfect Cell, he fought evenly against Goku and his son but was outmatched by Super Saiyan 2 Gohan, who awakened from his rage. Cell also claimed that the blast radius of his attack could destroy the entire solar system. Cell remained the most powerful villain in Dragon Ball until the arrival of Majin Buu.

Majin Buu was awakened by Babidi from his long slumber, becoming the final enemy of Dragon Ball Z. Majin Buu was the most powerful villain in Dragon Ball Z thanks to his overwhelming power and speed, his regenerative skills, and his ability to absorb attacks. Even as Good Buu, his most innocent form, he possessed the same combat power as Super Saiyan 3 Goku.

His power increased after being absorbed by his evil form, becoming Kid Buu, who was significantly stronger than Super Saiyan 3 Gotenks and surpassed Gohan, who had unlocked his potential. Majin Buu also destroyed the Earth and was only defeated by Goku's Spirit Bomb.

The main villain of Dragon Ball Daima, Gomah, was an insignificant character before gaining a power-up by receiving the Third Evil Eye. His magical power increases, and he becomes gigantic. Gomah's strongest qualities are his unlimited stamina and regeneration, which give him an advantage in battles of attrition. Yet, Gomah isn't an experienced fighter.

Gomah was inferior to an adult Super Saiyan 3 in raw strength, but the Evil Third Eye heals him and prevents him from getting tired and taking fatal damage, making him difficult to defeat. Additionally, the Third Eye continually strengthens Gomah, putting him ahead of the Majin Buu forms seen in Dragon Ball Z. Additionally, Gomah's strength depends on the Third Eye being active.

Baby Vegeta is one of the main villains of Dragon Ball GT. Although Baby Vegeta was weak in his base form when he parasitized Vegeta, their powers combined, and he easily surpassed Goku's Super Saiyan 3. However, his most powerful form was when he transformed into the Golden Great Ape.

As the Golden Great Ape, Baby Vegeta acquired incredible combat power, comparable only to that of Goku's Super Saiyan 4. However, Goku in GT possesses more experience and has trained more than his younger version in Dragon Ball Daima, who fought Gomah. This places Golden Great Ape's raw strength above Gomah's.

Super 17 is a fusion of the original Android 17 with a version created by Dr. Myuu in Dragon Ball GT. According to Gero, Android 17's original talent surpassed Cell, but he was born in an incomplete state, reaching his stronger version as Super 17 with improved stamina, strength, and endurance, which could match up to Goku's Super Saiyan 4.

Discover the mightiest mortal warriors in the Dragon Ball universe, ranked by their incredible strength, abilities, and impact on the series.

However, due to his ability to absorb ki, Super 17 increases his fighting power with every hit and overpowers Goku. Yet, Super 17's weakness is that he is vulnerable to attacks while absorbing ki. Super 17 not only fought a stronger Goku than the one who defeated Baby, but his absorption ability is also a valuable trump card.

While Hit is not an evil villain, he is a professional assassin from Universe 6 who has served as an antagonist facing Goku in Dragon Ball Super's tournaments. Hit's potential comes from his Time Skip ability, which allows him to dodge and launch surprise attacks. Hit defeated Vegeta and was on par with Super Saiyan Blue Goku when using Kaioken.

In terms of combat power, Hit hasn't shown his true abilities, as his techniques are meant to "kill" rather than fight. However, Hit is exceptionally fast and adapts to his opponent's rhythm quickly before defeating them with devastating attacks before they notice, which will make him capable of analyzing Super 17's weakness and killing him.

Omega Shenron is the result of Syn Shenron absorbing the other six Shadow Dragons' Dragon Balls, which is said to have multiplied his power by up to tenfold. This humanoid dragon was the strongest enemy the Z Fighters faced before Dragon Ball Super, as his negative energy gives him a destructive potential far greater than anything seen at the time.

Omega Shenron was able to defeat Goku and Vegeta in Super Saiyan 4. However, although Omega Shenron appears invincible, Goku and Vegeta combine their powers by fusing into Gogeta in Super Saiyan 4 to defeat him. Omega Shenron was completely outclassed by Gogeta, but he could cause trouble for Super 17 even in his base form, Syn Shenron.

And if you've been considering one for any of those situations, the Power 2000 is currently down to $749.99 from its original $1,299 price, taking nearly $550 off what would otherwise be a fairly expensive investment.

Performance-wise, DJI says the 2,048Wh capacity can keep a refrigerator running for up to 40 hours during a home power outage, charge a laptop 18 times, or power a projector for 18 hours. #3493. This Autonomous Camera Robot Is My New Best Friend

Like any pure-hearted geek, I've wanted to own a droid ever since I saw Star Wars as a kid. Now, I actually have one: It's Beni, a new gadget from Mondo Robotics, and it has me saying, "Artoo who?" It's not just my Upgrade of the Week; it's possibly the upgrade of my life.

Beni is an all-terrain camera robot that was born as a project on Kickstarter, but unlike so many other Kickstarted projects, it's actually really cool. It takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control it with a remote, or you can make it follow you. It can also be set to track you from the side or circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote control on the fly, so with minimal effort, there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's adorable. Just look at this little guy:

Being cute wouldn't matter if Beni was just a gimmick, but the footage it takes is actually really impressive. Check out this clip, which I recorded with no planning of any sort; I just locked Beni's camera on this skater and told it to follow him wherever:

See how smoothly it glides over the uneven concrete? How effortlessly it handles inclines? I even launched it off a huge ramp and it landed on the other side, righted itself, and got back to business.

Here's an example of the kind of footageyou'll get when you put it in "circle you" mode (and again, this was recorded with no prior planning):

The way it just slides under that bench? Come ON. That's just slick.

Yes, Beni is a slightly silly product, but as slightly silly products go, it's pretty inarguably awesome. Here is a short list of things I love about Beni:

It's super easy-to-use. I got it up and running moments after taking it out of the box and downloading the app. You can easily figure out how it works on the fly.

It's a multi-terrain robot. You can get an extra set of bigger, beefier wheels, but even with the stock tires, this thing worked great on uneven concrete, grass, and dirt.

It's rugged. While Beni does have obstacle detection ability, it runs into things a lot anyway, but that's not a problem. Beni can take massive, epic spills, slam into walls, and get kicked by children, and it will right itself and proceed on without a hitch. It's amazing to watch.

It actually works the way you expect it to. I know that's a low bar to clear, but it's rare for a flashy piece of tech to actually do what it says it promises, and Beni does.

It's adorable. A lot of work went into making Beni as friendly-looking as possible—it does tricks, blinks its "eyes," responds to gestures, and you can even give him a little baseball cap. Beni's vibe is positive.

It's great for social interaction. If you have a little robot following you around, people will want to talk to you. I'm not a huge fan of people, but if you want to make friends at the park, this robot will at least open the door.

It's not as expensive as you might imagine. Beni will run you $750 for the base model, and $899 for the "Explore Combo" with larger wheels, a charging stand, and a little hat. While $750 isn't cheap, for what you get, it's actually a pretty solid deal. Everything costs a fortune now anyway! You deserve a robot.

Beni isn't quite ready to make its debut yet. Right now, you can pre-order one on Mondo Robotics site, with a release planned for some time in early November. This is the company's first product, so it's not yet clear if Beni will ever be sold via third-party retailers like Amazon.

#3491. This Pricey New Accessory Gives Your Kindle a Feature That Used to Be Standard

It has been 14 years since Amazon made a Kindle e-reader without a touchscreen, and while I certainly don't miss the days of slowly paging through my e-book library with the arrow keys on my Kindle Keyboard, the move to touch navigation did have one unfortunate result, at least for a small subset of readers: the loss of physical page-turn buttons. Once standard on all Kindles, they eventually became a premium feature available only on the pricey Kindle Oasis, before being dropped from the lineup entirely when that device was retired in 2024.

While this fall's overhaul of the Kindle lineup introduced upgrades like a metal enclosure and a flush-front design, Amazon hasn't exactly reintroduced physical buttons, but the company has launched a new accessory to appeal to the roughly 5% of the market that loves buttons (per Kevin Keith, Amazon's vice president in charge of Kindle), which essentially turns your new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition into a Kindle Oasis: the Kindle Page-Turn Cover.

Releasing alongside the new flush-front Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, the Page-Turn Cover is made of plant-based leather (in one of three colors to match your Kindle—Graphite, Fig, or Seaglass Green) with a magnetic front flap, a soft interior, and a right-hand bezel made of lightly textured plastic that houses two thin, elongated buttons. When you slot your compatible Kindle into the case, connecting it magnetically and via the built-in pogo pins, it will automatically pair with the device, allowing you to turn pages with a button press instead of a tap.

By default, the top button will advance you forward by one page, and the bottom button will do the reverse, though you can change which does which in your device settings. While the physical buttons on some Boox and Barnes & Noble Nook devices allow you to map different functions—like skipping an entire chapter or scrubbing through a book quickly—to a long-press or double-tap, as of this writing, the Page-Turn Cover will only let you turn one page at a time. The buttons also only work for turning pages; you'll still navigate your library and the device menus using the touchscreen.

If you're a lefty, or prefer to swap which hand you use to hold your e-reader, you can change up the orientation by turning off Lock Rotation on your device; when you flip it over to hold in your other hand, the text will automatically reorient itself, and the buttons will continue to work with your existing settings.

You might think that changing pages with an accessory would slow down your device, but in my testing, the Page-Turn Cover actually seems to turn pages faster than tapping the touchscreen. Though the new Kindles are quite speedy, there's still a perceptible lag between when you tap the screen and when the display changes to a new page. Not so with the Page-Turn Cover attached; although the very first page turn after attaching it is a bit laggy, after that it is basically instantaneous. I can't imagine this will be a game-changer for anyone—the difference is a mere fraction of a second—but it's worth noting all the same.

While this is Amazon's clever solution to satisfy the physical button die-hards without overhauling the design of its entire lineup, it does come at a cost to the reader—a literal cost: The Page-Turn Cover is around $80, and it's only compatible with the $250 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition or the $320 Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, the only models with the metal backing, pogo pins, and accelerometer necessary for the case to function.

In short, that means if you want a Kindle with physical buttons, you'll have to shell out at least $330, or $80 more than the third-generation Kindle Oasis cost when it launched back in 2019. (For what it's worth, you can get the Oasis-like Boox Go 7, one of my picks for the top non-Kindle e-readers, for around $270).

While most people probably don't think twice about tapping the screen to turn the page, some folks just prefer the feel of tactile buttons or would rather not have to worry about holding their device wrong and accidentally jumping forward a chapter or two.

If you've made do without them so far, you probably aren't missing them, but if you're an old-school e-reader (or just a particularly tactile person), they are definitely a nice bonus. Are they worth an $80 upgrade? That's going to depend on the reader.

The year is almost over, and somehow we’ve already made it through Halloween and are heading straight into the Thanksgiving and holiday season. But no matter how busy things get, there’s always time to squeeze in a little anime.

November is a slightly quieter month for anime premieres, as most of the fall season’s biggest releases have already gotten underway, but that doesn’t mean there’s nothing worth checking out. Netflix is bringing us a couple of interesting new animated releases, including the long-awaited adaptation of Fool Night and the genre-bending Bass X Machina. Meanwhile, Crunchyroll keeps delivering new episodes of familiar favorites, with The Apothecary Diaries and Black Clover moving their stories forward. What would you do if you had the option to give up your humanity in exchange for a better life? Fool Night is the highly anticipated upcoming anime adaptation of Kasumi Yasuda’s manga. Set in a world where thick clouds have blocked out the sun for an entire century, humanity is struggling to survive. With most vegetation dead and oxygen becoming increasingly scarce, scientists have developed a process known as Transfloration, which turns people nearing the end of their lives into plants that can produce oxygen. Those who undergo the procedure become known as Spiriflor.

The story follows Toshiro Kamiya, a young man barely making ends meet while trying to support his sick mother. With mounting expenses and very few options left, he begins considering Transfloration as a way to escape his miserable circumstances. But giving up his human body comes with a pretty high cost.

Release Date: November 3 | Studio: Studio Mir | Streamer: Netflix

Technically, Bass X Machina isn’t a traditional anime, but we’re making room for it anyway. This upcoming adult animated series comes from South Korea’s Studio Mir, the acclaimed and fan-favorite animation studio behind titles like The Legend of Korra. After several delays, the project is finally making its way to Netflix, bringing a combination of Western action, steampunk aesthetics, and supernatural elements.

At the center of the story is a father who finds himself pushed to increasingly extreme measures when protecting his family means taking justice into his own hands. This incredible anime debuts on November 3 and promises a unique take on the ever-popular Western genre. It also has an incredible voice cast led by Oscar nominee Brian Tyree Henry.

Between strange illnesses and rumors that seem too unusual to ignore, she once again finds herself caught up in the middle of something far bigger than it initially lets on.

Meanwhile, Jinshi is adjusting to his new responsibilities as the Imperial Brother. His position comes with its own set of complications, particularly as rumors surrounding an immortal maiden and an approaching famine begin spreading throughout Li. And of course, the slow-burn romance between these two leads keeps on sizzling, giving fans small glimpses of their developing relationship.

Asta and Yuno are two childhood friends who grew up together with the shared dream of becoming the Wizard King. While Yuno was naturally gifted with magic, Asta was born without any magical abilities whatsoever. Rather than accept that his dream was impossible, Asta dedicated himself to physical training and eventually discovered a mysterious power of his own through a rare five-leaf Grimoire.

In Season 2, Black Clover is not only breaking streaming charts left and right, but also moving into another major chapter as the Clover Kingdom faces one of its greatest threats yet. With the Dark Triad wreaking havoc across the region, Asta and the Magic Knights are preparing for a dangerous mission into the Spade Kingdom. Their goal is to rescue their captured squad captains, but getting them back won’t be easy. Blue Box follows Taiki Inomata, a badminton player who spends much of his time training at school and admiring Chinatsu Kano, a talented basketball player who seems completely out of his league. Season 2 continues exploring the relationship between the two as they navigate their increasingly complicated feelings, but also, a fractured friendship from the past and some seriously tough competition threaten to complicate their personal lives and their respective journeys toward their individual goals as athletes. My backyard is looking spectacular with the autumnal tones of gold and russet leaves. And I don’t even mind as they drift onto my lawn, creating a beautiful carpet of color.

But while I’m happy for them to settle for a short while, I won’t leave them all through winter, because although I appreciate their current aesthetic, over time they’ll damage my lawn.

A light flurry of leaves is not so much of a problem, but once your lawn gets covered in a carpet of fallen leaves, it can harm its health if they are not removed.

A thick layer of leaves is an open invitation to fungal disease, as the decaying matter traps moisture, blocks airflow and starves the grass of sunlight. This dark and damp microclimate is the perfect environment for fungi to thrive.

The layer of fallen leaves acts like a blanket, holding in rain, dew and condensation. And once the leaves are left there for a prolonged period, snow mold, brown patch and leaf blight will develop.

If your lawn is lightly covered with leaves, you can leave them be. The wind may help disperse some, while the rest will decompose and add nutrients to the soil.

However, if your lawn is covered in a deep pile of leaves, there’s little chance of sunlight reaching the blades of grass, and the trapped moisture won't dry out. In this scenario, you need to grab a rake and remove the leaves to prevent disease from becoming rife. If you don’t fancy the workout that raking leaves provides or you want to save time, you could also opt for a leaf blower or lawn sweeper.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Besides being a magnet for fungal disease, if leaves are left on your lawn, they can also attract pests. The leaf canopy can provide cover, warmth, moisture, and, once the leaves break down, food.

This metal rake comes with an adjustable head that can expand from 7-23 inches to suit your task. This allows it to pick up large leaves, clippings and lawn debris with ease, and it's also small enough to fit under hedges.

Whether you choose to rake or mow over your leaves, always aim for dry conditions. But if the forecast doesn’t look promising, clear what you can anyway — leaving a layer of wet leaves will suffocate your lawn and invite disease.

If the leaf cover is light, rather than a thick carpet, mowing is the faster route. Just ensure the leaves aren’t soaked to avoid clogging your mower. Best of all, mowing your leaves turns them into a valuable organic mulch, putting the goodness back into your soil.

#3487. These Are the Best Arc Browser Alternatives, Now That It's Shutting Down

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Well, it happened: The Browser Company has finally announced that it will be sunsetting the Arc browser before the end of 2026. The writing has been on the wall for well over a year now: Arc had already been put on ice, receiving only maintenance updates after the Browser Company switched its focus to Dia, an AI browser that shares Arc’s framework but lacks the wonderful interface features that made Arc such a joy to use.

This is sad news for the Arc faithful. If you're one of them, or if you’re looking for an alternative to the regular browsers like Safari and Chrome, all hope is not lost. Export your Arc data, and try out one of these Arc-like alternatives.

Zen has become the de facto option for all users looking to find something that looks and works like Arc. In some ways, it’s better than Arc; in some ways it falls short.

I’ve been using Zen for months, and I’m quite happy with it. The only downside I can see is the Firefox web engine; while Gecko has come a long way, it can still sometimes fall short of Chromium, mostly because Google Chrome is such a popular browser, most websites are designed to run best on it. When I run into an issue with a website, I tend to switch to Chrome for a while. Zen can also sometimes be a memory hog, but once I got better at tab hygiene (automatically closing older tabs and being vigilant about workspace management), the experience got quite a bit better.

And yes, there is extension support: Anything that runs on Firefox will run here too. Firefox has most of the important extensions covered, and it’s the only major browser that still supports the full-scale uBlock Origin ad blocker (which works like a treat in Zen, too).

Alternatively, you can go to the opposite end of the spectrum and try out a maximalist browsing approac:. For a while, Microsoft Edge was the cleaner, faster, better version of Chrome, but now, that title goes to Vivaldi. Under the hood, Vivaldi uses the same Chromium engine that powers Google Chrome, so all your websites will work as expected, and all the extensions will be familiar. But Vivaldi is an extremely customizable browser, and for a certain kind of user, it might be the perfect fit.

There are tons of built-in features. It comes with an ad blocker and integrates with ProtonVPN for free, limited VPN access. You can add a free reader, email accounts, note-taking, and a calendar to the sidebar. Using the Web Panels feature, you can dock any website to the sidebar as well (this works well for media and messaging sites).

Vivaldi also has robust tab management features: You can use two websites in split screen (like with Zen and Arc), and you can organize tabs in workspaces. You can also group related tabs in Tab Stacks, Vivaldi’s unique two-level tab management system. One thing Vivaldi lacks by default is a vertical sidebar, which even Firefox and Chrome now support, though it can be added using a mod.

If you want to keep to a Chromium-based browser, but one that offers all the customization features you can think of, go for Vivaldi. At its core is a powerful, fast, and reliable browser that you can slowly remake to be your own.

Helium: Think of it as a minimalist version of Google Chrome. Same Chromium engine, but no Google tracker, no popups, ads, or extra features.

Dia: If you really want to use something that’s built by the same team as Arc, and don’t mind the AI features, you can try the Dia browser as well. It’s not an exact replacement, but Dia now has an option to use a vertical sidebar and pinned apps.

Quiche: If you were using Arc on iPhone or iPad, try using the Quiche browser, which is our favorite browser for the iPhone. It’s a tastefully designed independent browser, with a fully customizable layout.

#3486. Apple VP talks new iPad mini: OLED without ProMotion, Acoustic Display, more

Apple unveiled its “biggest update ever” for the iPad mini this week, introducing a thinner, lighter design and an OLED display.

In a pair of interviews, Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering, discussed the new iPad mini’s design, display, and more.

While the new iPad mini features an OLED display, it doesn’t support ProMotion. Instead, it’s limited to a 60Hz refresh rate. Here’s what Pakula had to say about that decision in an interview with Chris Lawley:

Display experience is about more than just a single spec. One of the things that’s really cool about OLED is it actually has this really fast pixel response time. So it’s more than an order of magnitude faster than the pixel response time for an LCD display.

What that does is it makes everything really smooth. Motion blur is significantly reduced compared to LCD. When you pair that with the other things, the contrast, the brightness, and the color, this is just a killer display.

In addition to being lighter and thinner, the new iPad mini is also IP67-rated for water and dust resistance, a first for an iPad. One key enabler is a new Acoustic Display. Pakula explains how that technology works:

One of the cool things we realized as we started experimenting was that the unique size and form factor of this display actually had a resonant frequency that’s in the audible range.

I think more importantly, it’s in the range of like a traditional woofer that you’d have in a speaker. What we did was we built these custom drivers that actually energize the display and emit sound directly through the enclosure, but that only really works for the mid and low frequencies.

For the higher frequencies, we actually designed these little custom tweeters. There’s one on each end of the product, and they’re actually ported out through these hidden ports between the glass and the aluminum. The result is we have this product that’s water and dust resistant. I think the sound that comes from it is so surprising for a form factor of this size.

Pakula also sat down with Katarina Mogus for an interview, where he discussed how the iPad mini fits into a world where iPhone Duo also exists:

What we love about the iPad mini is it’s really the full iPad experience in the palm of your hand. That gives you access to a million+ apps in the App Store. It’s got incredibly powerful creative accessories like the Apple Pencil Pro. And it’s got the advanced multitasking of iPadOS 27.

It is really incredibly universal. And honestly, with all these updates, all of those experiences just got so much better.

You can watch both interviews below. The new iPad mini is available to pre-order now, with the first orders arriving on November 6.

#3483. The Newest Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition Is Finally Worth the Extra Money

I love e-readers, but I'd be the first to admit that as far as the general public is concerned, they are just about the least exciting tech devices around—and that goes double for the Amazon Kindle. Any attention the space has gotten over the past couple of years has involved obscure players like Boox and weird concepts like the phone-shaped Palma or the tiny Boox Picco. But the clear leader in terms of market share is still Amazon, and despite some minor innovations over the years, the device hasn't received an essential upgrade in around a decade: A Kindle is a Kindle is a Kindle.

I'd still say this holds true in 2026, even after the company unveiled a complete redesign of the Kindle lineup (this, a few months after significantly raising prices across all of the devices). While the new flush-front display is nice-looking (and Amazon is quite proud of the new process it has developed to add colored bezels by painting them directly onto the outer glass screen), competitors have offered similar designs for years, and it's hard to get too excited about "innovations" like an $80 case that adds back the physical buttons that used to be built in or finally opening up the firmware to allow for the use of a Bluetooth page-turn remote.

But one thing has changed about the 2026 Kindle lineup: I think the $50 premium Amazon charges for the top-of-the-line Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft is finally truly justified.

Amazon introduced the first "Signature Edition" of the Kindle Paperwhite back in 2021, and while the 25% price increase didn't get you nothing, the features it did add weren't too exciting: At 32GB, it had three times the storage versus the standard Paperwhite, but how important is a ton of storage when most e-book files are tiny? (That's still enough room for more than 6,000 texts, well more than even true bookworms will read in an entire lifetime.) Other bonuses, like wireless charging and an auto-adjusting front light, won't matter at all to a huge subset of readers, and it's hard to think of "no ads on the lock screen" as an extra perk.

But the latest Signature Editions of the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft actually give you more for the price premium, and for the first time, I would recommend shelling out the extra cash. While the important specs are still the same as the standard model:

7-inch, 300ppi flush-front display (with color content on the Colorsoft maxing out at 150ppi)

USB-C charging with battery life "up to 12 weeks on a single charge," per Amazon

Bluetooth support for wireless headphones

...the Signature Editions give you quite a bit more this time around, including, most noticeably, a totally new design with an all-metal rear panel that gives the devices a much sleeker look and feel without adding much in the way of weight (the standard plastic models weigh around 7.2 ounces, while the Signature Editions weigh 8.1 ounces). The new design makes the Signature Editions feel truly premium.

But that's not the only meaningful addition. Once again, alongside wireless charging and automatically adjusting lighting, the Signature Editions have a boosted 32GB of storage, which is still probably overkill, but worthwhile if you like to load your device with a bunch of audiobooks or (in the case of the Colorsoft) color comics.

You also get an accelerometer, which means the display will auto-rotate if you flip it upside down, giving you more flexibility in how you hold it (especially if you're springing for the new Page-Turn Cover, which brings back physical buttons à la the beloved, discontinued Kindle Oasis). Moreover, there's a new ability to turn pages by double-tapping on the bottom sides or back of the device rather than touching the screen (though it only works for moving forward in your book).

Speaking of which, you'll need to go for the Signature Editions if you want to use accessories like the Page-Turn Cover or the also-new Charging Stand (not yet available for pre-order), as only the Signature Editions include the built-in magnetic pogo pins you'll need to connect them. (If you're interested in the Kindle Click page-turn remote, it at least works with any Kindle from 2024 or later.)

Finally, if you care about your Kindle looking pretty, it's worth noting that only the Signature Editions are available in Seaglass Green (for the Paperwhite) and the reddish-purple Plum (for the Colorsoft).

Outside of those extras, the 2026 Kindles don't feel much different than the 2024 models. According to Amazon, they are the fastest Kindles ever, but that's mostly hype—any recent Kindle will turn pages quickly enough that you'll barely notice the speed difference, if you notice it at all. They all still run on the same firmware, which is both a good thing (Amazon makes it extremely easy to browse for and buy books and audiobooks directly on the device; there are a ton of options to search through and sort your library; and quality-of-life features like being able to sideload books via email using the "Send to Kindle" feature are a godsend) and a bad thing (I hope you like being locked into the Amazon ecosystem).

One change to the entire 2026 Kindle lineup is already proving divisive: Judging by reactions on the Kindle Reddit, not everyone is in love with the new flush-front design, which eliminates the raised bezels around the screen that were present on the 2024 model, but at the cost of adding a thin layer of glass over the e-ink display.Depending on how picky you are, you may find fault with this setup, as the additional layer of glass slightly reduces text clarity by putting more distance and another barrier between your eyes and the text or images in your book. Is this something I noticed myself? No—I don't have an older Kindle to make a direct comparison, and the text is still much, much sharper (and the front lighting more even) than what I see on competing e-readers like the Boox Go 6 or the Xteink X4 Pro. But there is a contingent of readers already lamenting the change, so take that for what you will.

The question to consider whenever a new device model rolls around is simple: Is this worth the upgrade? If you have a working Kindle from any time after the introduction of temperature-adjustable lighting, I would say no—the 2026 models are nicer, but they still don't do anything to make them worth it, especially at the new higher price points. That said, if you are in the market for a new Kindle, I'd suggest opting for the Paperwhite over the entry-level model, which has a smaller screen and lacks the warm light option—and if you're getting a Paperwhite or Colorsoft, you might as well pay the premium for the Signature Edition, because it's finally worth the extra money.

#3482. ‘Bosch’ Meets ‘Mindhunter’ in Apple TV’s Gritty 10-Episode Serial Killer Thriller

Apple TV+ remains the go-to destination for the most gripping dramas on television. While viewers lament the lack of mysteries such as Bosch and Mindhunter recently, the detective series Nocturne is filling the void. Liev Schreiber takes up the archetypal mantle of a haunted detective, Jonah, who never got over the trauma of taking down serial killer Jurek Walter (Stephen Graham). The fallout of the case was so detrimental that Jonah lost not just his wife and child but his partner as well.

The stakes are high for Jonah when Walter’s crimes start to resurface. Even though he is locked away in a psychiatric facility, Walter’s supposed previous victim, young Michael Frost, is found wandering on a bridge. Held captive for three years, authorities question if and how Walter could be involved in this or if it is the work of a copycat or accomplice. Nocturne marries the interpersonal detective issues that were prevalent in Bosch with the gripping subject matter of serial killers found in Mindhunter. The best of both worlds, Nocturne particularly excels when it comes to its performances.

Stephen Graham has cultivated quite the career with characters on opposite ends of the spectrum. After portraying a father out of sorts in the intense and near-perfect miniseries, Adolescence, he is taking on a completely different role. Graham portrays Jurek Walter, the criminal supposedly behind the disappearance of Michael Frost. As Jonah attempts to figure out how Michael was released when Walter was incarcerated, Graham steals the show as said incarcerated criminal.

Jonah’s investigation and personal dynamics are compelling, but Nocturne truly shines when it comes to Graham’s scenes. He portrays the type of killer who Holden Ford would love to unpack on Mindhunter. As the case progresses, Walter shows how dangerous he is in his relationship with empathetic nurse Karl (Rory Culkin). Karl’s need for money puts him into a precarious situation when he accepts a new position of administering Walter’s medication.

With little training for this high-stakes job, Karl is an obvious target for Walter’s manipulative tendencies. The cat-and-mouse game between them is the highlight of the series, especially when it comes to Graham’s performance. While Nocturne adheres to many tropes of the detective genre, Graham rejects being compared to any other serial killer. He doesn’t have the bravado of Hannibal Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs; instead, he has a quiet eeriness that is chilling to watch.

Peel back the layers of Walter’s character, and viewers can see the monster capable of burying his victims alive. Graham is clearly the standout of the project, but is just one component of the multi-layered story. The ensemble cast of Liev Shrieber, Rory Culkin, Bill Camp, and Zazie Beetz all carry the story in a narrative with many twists and turns. Nocturne is the return to the detective genre that is always a crowd-pleaser, with 10 episodes to sustain the gripping Apple TV+ mystery.

#3481. Apple cuts App Store commission in Taiwan following regulatory discussions [U]

Apple today announced that it is lowering its standard App Store commission in Taiwan, following discussions with the country’s Fair Trade Commission. Here are the details.

Over the past year or so, Apple has faced mounting regulatory pressure on several of its App Store practices and rules worldwide, particularly those related to app distribution, payment processing, commission fees, and alternative options for developers.

In Japan and Brazil, in response to local competition rules and investigations, the company introduced alternative app marketplaces, third-party payment options, and revised commission structures.

In the European Union, Apple recently overhauled its App Store fees and business terms to address concerns raised by the European Commission following a lengthy back-and-forth over its compliance with the Digital Markets Act.

Just last week, an Australian federal judge ordered Apple to allow alternative app distribution and payment methods following its years-long legal battle with Epic Games. Apple plans to appeal.

And yesterday, South Korean regulators fined Apple approximately $15.5 million and ordered changes to its App Store policies over payment restrictions, app review practices, and discriminatory commissions.

Now, Taiwan is joining that list, though the changes announced today are considerably narrower. Apple today informed developers that, starting this Saturday, October 31, its standard commission on paid apps and in-app purchases will drop from 30% to 26% in the Taiwanese iOS and iPadOS App Store.

Apple said the change follows discussions with the Taiwan Fair Trade Commission, and added that “signing the updated terms by October 31 is not required to receive the benefit of these commission rate changes starting that date.”

The company also updated its Apple Developer Program License Agreement to reflect the new terms, with translated versions expected to be available within the next month.

To read Apple’s full announcement, follow this link.

Update: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:

“We’re making updates to the Taiwan storefront of the App Store following constructive discussions with the Taiwan Fair Trade Commission. These changes reflect our ongoing commitment to providing developers with a thriving marketplace and ensuring the App Store remains the safest, most trusted platform for users. We will continue to equip developers with the tools, resources, and support they need to build, grow, and scale successful businesses on the App Store.”

#3479. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

For its first few years, Wordle never repeated a solution. If you could remember ever seeing a certain word as a solution, it was guaranteed not to be that day's answer. But that changed in February of 2026, when the New York Times officially announced that previous solutions may be reused.

Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to today's Wordle.

#3478. Reddit will soon require an account for most content

Earlier today Reddit announced that it’s rolling out social media-style ‘For You’ feeds, but that wasn’t the only big news today. Reddit also now says that it’s going to start requiring a logged-in account for accessing most of its content.

Reddit on Thursday said it’s moving to become a primarily logged-in experience, marking one of the most significant shifts in its 21-year history.

Reddit has long championed the open web. Now, it’s pushing to build a more direct relationship with users while also protecting its data from increased scraping in the AI era.

Reddit co-founder and CEO Steve Huffman said in an interview that the change is being made to “improve its user experience, bolster its ads business and prevent bots from scraping its proprietary data.”

That’s going to kill a lot of their traffic from search and instantly remove a ton of content from AI summaries. Interesting move.

The plan is to start testing the new logged-in experience this quarter, but only outside the US to start. It will then roll it out more broadly around the world.

What will Reddit users without an account be able to access? Huffman acknowledges they’re still finalizing those details. Per Axios though, the Reddit homepage will still be accessible to everyone. And if you visit the site “via search engines or shared links,” you’ll still be able to access the content.

However, if you try to browse Reddit in any other way or visit a specific subreddit without being logged in, it sounds like that will no longer be possible.

What do you think of Reddit making this change? Let us know in the comments.

#3477. 'Angry Old Man' with Alcohol Issues Kills Two Roommates Over Ice Cream Argument

A 69-year-old Florida man was arrested Wednesday after allegedly shooting and killing his two roommates following an argument over ... wait for it ... ice cream!!!

Police say what started as a "dysfunctional living arrangement" took a deadly turn after one roommate apparently ate Mark Robinson's dessert.

According to the arrest affidavit, obtained by TMZ, Robinson, who owns the Ocala, Florida home, told police he'd been having ongoing issues with his two roommates, 69-year-old Charles Etheze and 78-year-old Michael Menkes ... and it sounds like tensions had been boiling over for weeks.

According to Ocala Police, Etheze had contacted law enforcement "several times over the past few weeks" over issues at the home.

During a news conference, Ocala Police Chief Mike Balken described the situation as a "dysfunctional living arrangement." No kidding ... considering Robinson claimed he'd been dealing with ongoing problems involving his roommates, including their alleged failure to pay rent.

Balken didn't exactly paint Robinson as the friendliest guy in the neighborhood, either.

"It's clear that the homeowner, quite frankly, was an angry old man that had some alcohol problems and could get nasty with not only his neighbors but his tenants as well," Balken said.

Police say officers responded to the home at least three times this year ... but Wednesday's incident turned fatal.

According to the docs, officers were dispatched to the Ocala home after Robinson called police to complain that one of his roommates had eaten his ice cream. Yes, seriously.

"I have a very young officer trying to calm three 60, 70-year-old men down over ice cream. It's a ridiculous situation to happen," Balken said.

It's unclear exactly who ate Robinson's ice cream ... but the argument allegedly spiraled into something far more serious after officers left.

According to the arrest affidavit, Robinson admitted he'd been drinking that day, telling investigators he'd consumed a bottle and a half of wine before the shooting.

The docs say, after police left, Etheze and Menkes went for a walk, which Robinson described as part of their normal routine. But Robinson claimed he worried things would escalate when they returned, so he grabbed his Benelli 12-gauge shotgun and brought it into the living room because he "felt like there was going to be trouble."

Robinson told investigators that when the two men returned, they made a comment referring to themselves as the "ice cream bandits" before allegedly rushing toward him.

He claimed Etheze had a knife in his hand ... prompting Robinson to pick up his shotgun and fire a round, striking Etheze in what he believed was the front side of his body.

Robinson said he fired a second shot when Etheze attempted to get back up.

But here's where his story gets even more interesting.

Police say they didn't find Etheze in the living room, where Robinson initially claimed the confrontation happened. Instead, officers say they found him in a hallway outside the home.When investigators questioned Robinson about the inconsistency, they say he admitted Etheze had retreated into the hallway after the first shot ... and Robinson followed him before firing a second round.

As for his other roommate, Menkes ... he allegedly tried to make a run for it, but apparently didn't get very far.

Per the docs, Robinson told investigators Menkes was attempting to escape through the front door and had made it outside toward the front gate when Robinson shot him in the back.When police asked why he fired at Menkes as he was fleeing, Robinson claimed he believed Menkes was going to "come after him."

During the news conference, Balken said Robinson was already known around the neighborhood for being "cantankerous" with neighbors and children.

Robinson is now claiming self-defense ... but it doesn't look like authorities are buying his version of events, at least for now.

He's been arrested on one count of second-degree murder, though investigators say additional charges are possible.

And things didn't seem to go smoothly during his first court appearance, either ... it appears Robinson refused to sign the judge's findings at the initial hearing concerning the charges against him.

The VR headset may be becoming a thing of the past. At Google's Android Developer Summit this morning, XReal officially debuted XReal Aura XR glasses, smart glasses with full XR capability. The result: Aura packs a 70° field of view in a pair of glasses that weigh less than 95 grams.

Customers in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea can order XReal Aura on XReal's site starting today, and they're expected to begin shipping in mid-November. The limited-time launch price is $1,099 for the 12GB + 256GB configuration and $1,299 for the 16GB + 512GB configuration, $180 and $200 less, respectively, than XReal announced earlier this month. The lower prices will be available until the end of the year.

If the claim of mixed reality in a pair of sunglasses seems dubious, I tried them out a few months ago, and they are exactly that.

Instead of an enclosed headset, XReal Aura projects digital content on transparent lenses so you can be present in the real world while also in the digital world. Unlike "traditional" virtual reality headsets, the Aura's batteries and main compute are in a wired puck/controller you can slip into your pocket. That keeps the weight down and makes them comfortable enough to wear for longer periods. Because it's built on Android XR, users will have access to millions of 2D and 3D Android apps right out of the box.

If you want to go beyond Android, you can plug a USB-C-compatible computer or gaming console into Aura, and use that device in the same virtual space as native Android XR apps.

XReal Aura is launching with a library of over 150 "made for XR" apps as well, including games like Nevatars, designed by Andy Serkis, Fallout: Factions, a dice-based head-to-head game in the Fallout universe, and Landing Party, "the world's first outdoor roleplaying video game." There will also be companion apps for the NBA, NASCAR, and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s The Nutcracker. In terms of productivity, ShapexXR, a platform for software developer collaboration, is making its debut on Android XR, and you'll be able to use apps like Frontline.io for job training and assistance, and Plynk Spatial for stock research and trading.

If you want to get down to the nitty-gritty, here are the Aura's specs:

Split-compute architecture with compact compute puck

Wired Mirroring for laptops and compatible handheld gaming devices

USB-C connectivity using a standard connection

Electrochromic dimming for more immersive viewing

Support for voice, hand, keyboard, trackpad, and game controller input
